summary: Describes requirements for multi-segment pseudowires, which extend the reach of pseudowires across multiple domains. The domains can be autonomous systems under one or several providers, IGP areas, or administratively set up pseudowire domains. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire is a virtual wire. This lists what is needed to join several virtual wire pieces into one longer wire that crosses networks.

questions: what is an s-pe in pwe3
why use ms-pw instead of ss-pw
subtitle: What a pseudowire solution must do to stretch one virtual wire across several networks, joined end to end.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire normally runs between two provider edge routers over one packet network. Providers sometimes need one wire to cross several domains, but a direct connection between the end routers may be impossible, unsafe or unscalable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines multi-segment pseudowires (MS-PWs): several ordinary pseudowire segments joined at switching provider edges (S-PEs). It then lists requirements for setup, resiliency, quality of service, congestion control, routing, OAM, management and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol. It tells solution designers what an MS-PW mechanism has to provide.

today: RFC 5254 is an Informational document, published in October 2008, and the registry shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only; it does not itself define a protocol.

sections.title: Scope and Reference Models
sections.content:
This document sets requirements for multi-segment pseudowires (MS-PWs): pseudowires that cross more than one packet switched network (PSN) domain or more than one PSN tunnel. Single-segment pseudowires (SS-PWs), which run edge to edge across a single PSN domain, are covered by RFC 3916. The document is not meant to invalidate any part of RFC 3985, and its requirements do not apply to PSNs that only support SS-PWs.

The domains in question can be autonomous systems under one provider, IGP areas in one autonomous system, autonomous systems of two or more providers, or administratively established pseudowire domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Some wires only need one hop. This memo is about wires that need several hops joined together to cross different networks.

sections.title: Terminating and Switching Provider Edges
sections.content:
An MS-PW is a static or dynamically configured set of two or more contiguous PW segments that behave as a single point-to-point PW. Each end must terminate on a T-PE (terminating provider edge), where the customer attachment circuits are bound to a PW forwarder.

Between them sit one or more S-PEs (switching provider edges). An S-PE switches the control and data planes of the preceding and succeeding segments, and terminates the PSN tunnels that carry them. It switches from one segment to another based on the PW identifiers, such as the PW label for MPLS PWs. A switching point is never both the S-PE and the T-PE for the same MS-PW.

Segments of the same MS-PW may use the same or different PW types and PSN technologies, but this document requires support only for MS-PWs whose segments are all of the same PW type. In the inter-provider example, an MS-PW from one autonomous system to another has three segments: one inside the first AS, one between the two border routers, and one inside the second AS.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends of the long hose plug into the houses. The joints in the middle are special connectors that pass the water along from one piece to the next.

sections.title: Why Multi-Segment Pseudowires
sections.content:
The RFC says single-segment pseudowires are enough in the vast majority of cases. MS-PWs may help in these situations:

  • Inter-provider PWs: the two terminating PEs sit in different provider domains.
  • No direct control channel: a T-PE may not be allowed to learn or reach the remote T-PE address, and a single contiguous PSN tunnel between domains may be undesirable for security or scalability reasons. An MS-PW also lets providers confine MD5 key administration for the LDP session to the switching points between two domains.
  • PSN interworking: the networks may use different PW signaling or PSN types, so the switching points do the interworking.
  • Traffic engineered tunnels: with bandwidth-managed PWs, a single-segment design would need a full mesh of PSN TE-tunnels. MS-PWs allow a sparse mesh or smaller PWE3 domains.
  • Access and metro networks: access elements need signaling adjacencies only with the PEs they connect to, not with every other access device.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you cannot run one hose all the way, because the neighbors do not trust each other or there are too many houses. Joining shorter hoses solves that.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC assumes three setup mechanisms: static configuration of every segment, a pre-determined route set up with end-to-end signaling and automated stitching at S-PEs, and a signaled dynamic route chosen with the help of routing protocols. Requirements that apply to all three include:

  • PWs MUST stay transparent to P-routers, and an MS-PW MUST be composed of SS-PWs using the same encapsulation modes.
  • Both directions of a segment MUST terminate on the same S-PE or T-PE.
  • Resiliency: mechanisms to protect an MS-PW when an element fails MUST be provided. Backup PWs and switchover on failure SHOULD be supported, and automatic revert MAY be provided but MUST be configurable.
  • Setup is successful only when all segments are set up.
  • Admission control against PSN tunnel resources MUST be done at each segment and MUST be configurable.
  • MS-PWs MUST be able to cross multiple provider domains and multiple autonomous systems.

Signaled segments must support the four SS-PW setup methods: static setup, LDP with PWid FEC 128, LDP with generalized PW FEC 129, and L2TPv3. For dynamic routing, routing must let PEs discover S-PEs on the path and MUST support re-routing around failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist says the joints must be invisible to the pipes in between, there must be a spare route if one breaks, and the hose only counts as working when every piece is connected.

sections.title: Quality of Service, Congestion, OAM and Management
sections.content:
Each S-PE maps a PW segment to a PSN tunnel. Solutions MUST let S-PEs and T-PEs bind a segment to a tunnel automatically based on class of service (CoS) and bandwidth, and MUST let them mark PW packets with a CoS value and translate CoS maps at domain boundaries. Following RFC 3985, MS-PWs MUST NOT transmit across unprovisioned best-effort paths without another congestion control scheme, and S-PEs are required to reject segments that cannot meet this. Congestion notification between PEs along the path MUST be possible, and a PE that knows a link or tunnel is congested MUST NOT set up new MS-PWs over it.

For operations and maintenance (OAM), MS-PW OAM MUST provide at least the capabilities of SS-PW OAM, and PW OAM segments can run T-PE to T-PE, T-PE to S-PE, or S-PE to S-PE. Defects on a PSN tunnel MUST be propagated to all PWs using it, and an S-PE MUST pass T-PE to T-PE OAM messages transparently. For management, MS-PWs MUST offer at least the capabilities SS-PWs have under RFC 3916, MIB tables MUST ease configuration at S-PEs and T-PEs, and remote management MUST be possible but SHOULD be disableable.
sections.plainLanguage: The hose must carry enough water for its job, tell everyone along the way when it is clogged, and let the plumbers find which piece is broken.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC separates inter-provider MS-PWs from intra-provider ones. For the data plane, an S-PE or T-PE SHOULD discard a packet from a neighbor across a provider border unless its MPLS labels were distributed to that neighbor, or to a peer beyond it. An S-PE at a domain boundary MUST be able to police incoming MS-PW traffic, MUST guard against packets marked for better CoS than they should receive, and MUST be configurable not to accept labeled packets from another provider unless the bottom label is a PW label it assigned on that interface. The document places no requirement on encrypting MS-PW packets, noting that encryption may be needed at a higher layer.

For the control plane, segments across a provider border SHOULD end on ASBRs, ideally joined by a physically secure link. Strong authentication MUST be implemented, including a signature on each individual setup message. A request MUST NOT be accepted unless its source address belongs to an eligible peer, and border S-PEs MUST be able to rate-limit signaling to resist denial of service. Manual key management is expected to be enough, but if large-scale connection to S-PEs in other ASs is needed, a mechanism based on RFC 4107 MUST be developed. For intra-provider MS-PWs the data path requirements for inter-provider ones also apply in such cases, to limit the impact of a compromised T-PE.
sections.plainLanguage: When hoses from different neighbors meet, you only accept water from people you know, check the labels on every connector, and put a limit on how much can come in.
